---
title: "Comparing one-cycle videos"
subtitle: "The same 104 recordings folded twice — once on the FIR band-pass phase, once on the M-SSA phase — 10 bins, five successive cycles, and a shuffled phase to tell us what any of it is worth"
include-in-header: figures_one_cycle_compare/plotlyjs.html
---

The [previous page](data-pulse-extraction-methods.qmd) compared seven ways of
getting a cardiac **phase** out of a registered B-scan video, and ranked them by
how well each agreed with the FIR band-pass. That ranking presupposed its own
answer: it scored every method against FIR, so FIR could not lose.

This page asks the question the pipeline actually needs answered. The phase is
never the deliverable either — the **folded video** is, and the choroidal
thickness curve read off it. So take the two most distinct methods from that
page, fold the video with each, and judge the *result*.

Nothing here is recomputed. The pulses and the phases are read straight out of
the `.npz` files the previous page's batch script wrote. The two folds get the
same frames, the same uniform time grid, the same 10 bins, the same median
folding and the same set of retained frames. **Only the phase differs**, so every
difference below is attributable to the phase and to nothing else.

::: {.callout-important}
## This run answers the question the 30-bin run raised

An earlier pass over **exactly these recordings, this registration and these
phases** cut the cycle into 30 bins. It concluded that the binding constraint was
not the phase method but the number of frames averaged per bin, and that two of
the obvious quality metrics were tracking the bin count rather than the
heartbeat. This run tests that directly by changing only the bin count — 30 → 10,
so roughly 46 frames per bin instead of 15.

The prediction holds, and then some. Split-half reproducibility on the thickness
curve goes from 0.017 to **0.212** for the FIR phase; peak-to-peak ΔY falls from
3.81 px to 1.65 px and its shuffled null falls with it, 4.10 → 1.61; modulation
depth halves, 0.057 → 0.031, identically for a real phase and a random one. Where
the 30-bin run found FIR indistinguishable from noise on every measure, **both
phases now clear the null on the tests that matter.**
:::

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/tab_cohort.qmd >}}

## Ten bins, and what that buys

The cycle is cut into **10 phase bins**, so a median recording puts about **46
frames in each** (459 frames folded, 10 bins) — and about 23 per bin once the
recording is split in half for the reproducibility test. That is the resolution
this page is measured at, and it is the single most important number on it.

At this bin count **no condition in the cohort has an empty bin**, against two at
30 bins. The smallest bin of a median recording holds 38 frames, and the
bin-count coefficient of variation is 0.10 for both real phases against 0.12 for
the null. Nothing on this page is reduced by missing bins; the `NaN` handling
that mattered at 30 bins is still in place and simply never fires.

## Five cycles, one per fifth of the recording

The delivered video is no longer a single averaged cycle. The recording is cut
into **five consecutive time slices** and each is folded on its own, so the video
runs five cycles back to back: the first is the first fifth of the acquisition,
the last is the last fifth. Each slice contributes about nine frames per bin.

This is a *visual* diagnostic, not a new statistic. A pulsation that is real and
stable gives five cycles that look alike; a phase that drifts, or a choroid that
moves for reasons unrelated to the heartbeat, shows up as five cycles that do
not. Watching one averaged cycle can never reveal that — it has already averaged
the evidence away.

Every number on this page is still measured on **one** cycle folded over the
whole recording. Redefining the metrics slice by slice would be a different
indicator, not a rescaling of this one, and it is not what is reported here.

## The one thing that makes these numbers readable

A folded video always looks plausible. Average forty-six B-scans into each of ten
bins and you get ten very clean B-scans, whatever phase you used to sort them —
so "the video looks good" is not evidence of anything. If anything, this run
looks *better* than the 30-bin one for a reason that has nothing to do with
timing: more frames per bin is a better speckle average.

Every measurement is therefore run a third time on a **shuffled phase**: the FIR
phase, randomly permuted over the uniform grid, carried through the identical
resampling and folding. Same frames, same bins, same everything — no timing. It
is the only scale these numbers have.

Three quantities are measured, all of them on both real phases and on the null:

- **split-half reproducibility** — the first half of the recording and the second
  are folded separately and the two cycles correlated, after removing each one's
  temporal mean so that the static anatomy (identical either way, and enough on
  its own to push any correlation towards 1) cannot contribute. A phase that
  tracks the heartbeat gives the same cycle twice; a phase that does not gives
  two independent noises. Measured on three representations of the same cycle —
  per pixel, on the column-averaged depth profile, and on the thickness curve —
  because they have very different signal-to-noise, and only their agreement is
  worth reading.
- **ΔY** — amplitude of the folded thickness curve, obtained by folding the
  *masks* with the same phase, read both as a raw peak-to-peak and as the
  amplitude of a 1-harmonic fit. This is the quantity the rigidity coefficient is
  built on.
- **bin occupancy** — how evenly the ten bins fill.

## One condition, two phases

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f1_thickness_ref.qmd >}}

Solid lines are the whole recording; dotted lines are each half folded on its
own. The gap between a method's two dotted curves is its split-half error, drawn
rather than summarised.

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f2_bins_ref.qmd >}}

Bin occupancy is close to uniform for both, which is what a phase that advances
at a roughly constant rate produces. It is a sanity check, not a discriminator:
the shuffled null fills the bins evenly too, by construction.

## The two phases are not the same phase

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f3_phase_agreement.qmd >}}

The phase comparison does not depend on the binning, so this section is identical
to the 30-bin run: it is a property of the two estimators, not of the video they
produce.

The two phases sit within 30° of each other — under a twelfth of a cycle — in
**68 of 104 conditions**. In **25** they are more than a quarter-cycle apart, and
in **15** more than 150° apart. Nine of those fifteen hold that near-inversion
with a phase-locking value above 0.5: a *stable* half-cycle offset, not
jitter. For those recordings the two videos are the same cycle played half a
period out of step — one shows the choroid filling where the other shows it
emptying.

The phase-locking value, which measures whether the offset at least stays
constant, has a median of **0.63**, and **88 of 104** conditions fall below 0.9.

What the binning *does* change is the agreement between the two folded videos:
they now correlate at a median of **0.18**, against 0.07 at 30 bins, and 70 of
104 fall below 0.3. Coarser bins do not make the two methods agree about the
choroid — they leave three times more frames in each bin to average the speckle
away, so the agreement that was there becomes visible. The two methods still
produce two different videos; it is now possible to see how different.

## Does either phase beat a shuffled one?

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f4_split_half_null.qmd >}}

**Both do, on the tests with the power to show it** — which is the headline
change from 30 bins, where FIR cleared nothing.

Against its own per-condition null (Wilcoxon signed-rank over the 104 paired
differences):

| measured on | FIR band-pass | M-SSA |
|:--|--:|--:|
| split-half, per pixel | **$p = 0.004$** | **$p = 7\times10^{-5}$** |
| split-half, thickness curve | **$p = 0.001$** | **$p = 0.049$** |
| split-half, depth profile | $p = 0.76$ | $p = 0.083$ |
| ΔY, 1-harmonic fit | $p = 0.22$ | **$p = 0.002$** |
| ΔY, peak-to-peak | $p = 0.96$ | $p = 0.060$ |

The absolute values matter more than the $p$-values, and this is where the run
differs most from its predecessor. The median split-half correlation on the
thickness curve is **0.212** (FIR) and **0.068** (M-SSA) against **0.055** for
the shuffled phase. At 30 bins those three numbers were 0.017, 0.026 and 0.027 —
the null nominally ahead of both. Tripling the frames per bin moved the FIR
thickness curve from indistinguishable-from-noise to twelve times its own null.

That is a real, reproducible cardiac cycle in the thickness curve, and it is the
first time this comparison has shown one.

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/tab_methods.qmd >}}

One row of that table still deserves to be read as a warning rather than a
result. **Modulation depth is identical for all three columns** — 0.031, 0.033,
0.033 — including the shuffled phase, exactly as it was identical at 0.057 across
the board at 30 bins. It halved when the bins tripled in size, in lockstep across
a real phase and a random one. It measures the bin count, not the heartbeat, and
it should not be used to judge a fold. It is kept here precisely to say so.

## FIR against M-SSA

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f4b_split_half_paired.qmd >}}

Head to head, the two methods now split the honours rather than one dominating:

| measured on | FIR ahead in | Wilcoxon $p$ |
|:--|--:|--:|
| split-half, per pixel (~3×10⁶ points) | 39 % of conditions | **0.039** (favours M-SSA) |
| split-half, thickness curve | 62 % | 0.077 (favours FIR) |
| split-half, depth profile | 49 % | 0.30 |
| ΔY, 1-harmonic fit | 41 % | **0.007** (favours M-SSA) |
| ΔY, peak-to-peak | 45 % | 0.087 |

M-SSA keeps the per-pixel test and both ΔY readings; FIR leads on the thickness
curve, at 62 % of conditions and $p = 0.077$ — suggestive, not established. The
honest summary is that **the choice between them no longer looks decisive at this
resolution**, which is itself a change: at 30 bins nothing favoured FIR anywhere.

The methodological caveat from that run stands. The previous page ranks M-SSA
below FIR by scoring it against a reference *defined* as the FIR pulse, which
penalises any departure whether it moves towards the truth or away from it. Read
on the folded video against a null instead, M-SSA is at worst FIR's equal.

## What this costs downstream

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f5_deltaY.qmd >}}

Read as **peak-to-peak of the folded thickness curve — the raw max minus min over
the ten bins — ΔY still does not beat the shuffled phase**:

| | FIR band-pass | M-SSA | shuffled (null) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| median ΔY peak-to-peak (px) | 1.65 | 1.77 | 1.61 |
| beats its own null in | 49 % of conditions | 60 % | — |
| Wilcoxon $p$ vs null | 0.96 | 0.060 | — |

FIR is a coin flip against its own null; M-SSA misses significance. But look at
what the bin count did to the numbers themselves: **3.81 → 1.65 px for FIR, and
4.10 → 1.61 px for the null.** Same recordings, same registration, same phases,
same choroid — only the number of frames averaged per bin changed, and the
"amplitude" more than halved. Peak-to-peak is an extreme-value statistic:
max-minus-min over noisy bins grows with the noise, so it inflates for a phase
that scatters frames at random exactly as it does for one that sorts them
correctly. It is a noise meter with a physiological name.

The signal survives once the curve is reduced to its fundamental. Fitting one
harmonic to the ten points before taking the amplitude gives **0.85 px** (FIR)
and **0.91 px** (M-SSA) against **0.50 px** for the null. Those three numbers
barely moved when the bins tripled in size (0.87 / 0.97 / 0.64 px at 30 bins),
while the peak-to-peak halved. **An estimator that is invariant to an arbitrary
analysis parameter is measuring something; one that tracks it is measuring the
parameter.**

The practical consequence for the rigidity coefficient is unchanged and now
better supported: **ΔY should be taken from a harmonic fit of the folded curve,
never from its peak-to-peak range** — and folded into ten bins rather than
thirty, since the finer resolution bought nothing and cost the reproducibility of
the thickness curve an order of magnitude.

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f6_bin_uniformity.qmd >}}

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/f7_disagreement_cost.qmd >}}

Where the two phases disagree most — low phase-locking value, on the left — the
split-half gain of one over the other scatters symmetrically about zero. The
disagreement does not resolve in favour of either method; it is simply where
both are least determined.

## All 104 videos, five cycles each

Every condition has its own page, carrying three things: the comparison video
(FIR on top, M-SSA below, both folded from the same frames, **five successive
cycles**); **ΔY along the folded cycle**, with the shuffled null superimposed on
the two real phases; and **the two pulses overlaid, their phase, and the
instantaneous heart rate** on the full recording, which is where a phase that
loses the beat becomes visible.

The five cycles are worth watching in sequence rather than as a loop: they are
five different fifths of the acquisition, not five repeats of one measurement.

{{< include figures_one_cycle_compare/_table.qmd >}}

## Conclusion

- **Bin count was the binding constraint, and this run proves it.** Same
  recordings, same registration, same phases; 30 bins → 10 bins takes the FIR
  split-half correlation on the thickness curve from 0.017 (below its null) to
  **0.212** (twelve times its null, $p = 0.001$). The 30-bin verdict that
  "the folded cycle is not reproducible for either phase" was a statement about
  the analysis, not about the data.
- **Both phases now beat a shuffled one** on the per-pixel and thickness-curve
  split-half tests. M-SSA additionally clears the null on the harmonic-fit ΔY
  ($p = 0.002$); FIR does not ($p = 0.22$).
- **Neither method is clearly preferable at this resolution.** M-SSA wins per
  pixel ($p = 0.039$) and on both ΔY readings ($p = 0.007$); FIR leads on the
  thickness curve without reaching significance ($p = 0.077$). This is a change
  from 30 bins, where nothing favoured FIR.
- **How ΔY is read still decides whether there is any signal.** Peak-to-peak does
  not beat a shuffled phase and halved when the bin count changed (3.81 → 1.65
  px, its null 4.10 → 1.61); the 1-harmonic fit beats it for M-SSA and barely
  moved (0.87 → 0.85 px). Use the fit, on ten bins.
- **Two metrics still track the analysis rather than the physiology.** Modulation
  depth is identical for a real phase and a random one at both bin counts (0.057
  at 30, 0.031 at 10), and peak-to-peak ΔY follows the bin count as faithfully
  for the null as for the signal. Any metric proposed for this pipeline should be
  run against the null, at more than one bin count, before it is trusted.

::: {.source-note}
Videos and tables produced by `Astronauts/compute_one_cycle_compare_methods.py`
(104 conditions, 14 astronauts, masks and registration
`model1_scale_1.0_flatten_choroid_xcorr`, **10 bins**, **5 cycles** — the record
cut into five consecutive slices, each folded separately — median folding, one
cardiac cycle trimmed at each end of the record for both methods alike). The
delivered video therefore holds 5 × 10 images, played at 10 fps so that one cycle
lasts about one second; the metrics are all measured on a *single* cycle folded
over the whole recording (`cycle_1` in the script), never on the five-slice cube.
No condition had an empty bin at this resolution. Pulses and phases are read from
`pulse_from_data/traces/<slug>.npz` and never re-estimated. Figures,
per-condition pages and the link table are generated by
`figures_one_cycle_compare/make_figures.py`, which only reads the three CSVs, the
per-condition `.npz` and the videos. Everything lives under `E:/NASA_Rigidity/`.
Re-run the figure script rather than editing the generated fragments (`f*.qmd`,
`tab_*.qmd`, `_table.qmd`, `one_cycles/oc_*.qmd`) by hand — and run it from the
repository root, not from inside `figures_one_cycle_compare/`, which is a
junction to `E:` and would send the per-condition pages there. The 104 comparison
videos now weigh **519 MB** in total (83 MB at 30 bins): five cycles instead of
one, at a lower frame rate. This page inlines `plotly.js` (4.9 MB) in its header;
the 104 per-condition pages load it from one shared `plotly.min.js` that the
browser caches once. All figures, here and there, are interactive.
:::
